In chemistry, the basicity of amines is determined by their ability to donate the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom. When comparing aromatic amines (like aniline) to aliphatic amines, we need to consider the effects of the aromatic ring on the nitrogen's electron pair.

The key difference is that in aniline (C6H5NH2), the nitrogen's lone pair can participate in resonance with the aromatic ring. This resonance causes the lone pair to be partially delocalized into the ring, making it less available for protonation. Additionally, the phenyl group (C6H5-) has an electron-withdrawing effect through resonance, which further decreases the electron density on the nitrogen.

In contrast, aliphatic amines (like methylamine, CH3NH2) don't have this resonance effect, so their lone pair is more localized on the nitrogen and more available for protonation, making them stronger bases.

Therefore, aromatic amines like aniline are weaker bases than aliphatic amines due to the electron-withdrawing effect of the phenyl group through resonance, which corresponds to option C.
